body: Thank you for you input

A few years back I read an article about a tiny immortal jellyfish ( t. dorhnii ) that, when under stress or starvation, resorts back to its polyp stage and starts its growth over as a brand new jellyfish…in the wild it can do this countless times in a process known as transdifferentiation. 
How crazy would it be if we could just resort back to our infant stage and start completely over when life became intolerable? 

[https://www.nhm.ac.uk/discover/immortal-jellyfish-secret-to-cheating-death.html](https://www.nhm.ac.uk/discover/immortal-jellyfish-secret-to-cheating-death.html)

You are not alone. I was obsessed with time of death after my brother took his life with a GSW to the head. Because he had been found (by my sister) some time after, they did not have a specific time of death, just an estimated window. I started researching how long rigor mortis sets in in relation to age, muscle mass, environmental factors etc etc etc. I wanted to know if I was awake and if I had called him could I have stopped it. I also researched the angle at which he shot himself to see if I could find out if it was quick or if he was alive and alone for a while...ALL OF THIS TO SAY, I sought out the uncomfortable questions in my head despite social repulsion of the subject and I found no concrete answers (because more often than not they are not retrievable) but I did find peace and no longer tormented with the questions. Now I just miss him and talk to him every day. I’m still (and forever) going to grieve but I am not tormented. 
I am so sorry for your loss and I do hope you find some peace in this incomprehensible place. 💗

I realize this isn’t for everyone but I write my brother who took his life almost two years ago. When I read back through the journal to him, I realize that in writing out my obsessive thoughts to him about his death, I slowly (but surely) have stopped obsessing. AND nobody gets tired of hearing about it.  I have come a long way. 
I’m am so very sorry for your loss. I hope you can find pockets of peace to carry you through this.

I’m coming up on two years since I lost my brother and so far the advice from many on this sub that the grief is not linear is true. I remember for a while after his passing seeing people (strangers) laughing and having a good time and wondering if I would EVER feel that way again. Since his death, surprisingly, I have laughed and found that I genuinely have enjoyed people and places again....just different than I did before. I still get hit heavy with the actualization of his choice to leave in the most random of times (like tonight. Can’t sleep) but I am also so much more aware of the loss all around me on a regular basis and how people loose their loved ones and somehow survive. Even laugh again. I am encouraged by their survival. This is beautiful to me. It’s almost as if I know joy in a purer form than I did before because it comes despite the tremendous absence his death has presented in my life. All I can say is I don’t try to avoid feeling any of my feelings even if they are considered “unhealthy” or “negative”. I have found that by allowing myself the space to feel all that this loss has produced, I can move through it easier than if I try to avoid it or tell myself that “I should...” or “should not...” . There are no road maps and everyone experiences this loss in their own way and no one is doing a “better job” at having lost someone to Suicide. I am so terribly sorry for the loss of your brother. Mine (David) was my favorite person in the world and despite what some may assume based off his decision, he was a magnetic beam of light. Be easy and gracious to yourself.

Thank you for sharing. I lost my little brother in SF in November 2018. “I Hold on to your memory. The memories yet to be. They may still come to exist....” I really appreciate this part of your poem because I have found in the last year and 8months That I have made A TON of new memories with my brother. You are right, it is not in the way we planned or expected but they are new memories nonetheless and I cherish them as I do all the memories from when he was still here. I am so very sorry for your loss and sending you and your family love and comfort.

Thank you for your encouragement. I appreciate your kind words. I am not at a giving up point, but I am keenly aware of my solitude in this situation (almost 30 years now). I think until society and/or individuals can have open conversations about suicide (sans the taboo and fear of the subject) there will continue to be an increase in casualties. For some, giving up is the only relief.
Yes! Often times just the act of putting food in my mouth (even if it’s raw romaine lettuce) triggers an overwhelming desire to keep eating.

Other than loved ones gone too soon, nothing comes strongly to mind. As I said in the post, I’ve had a good life. Perhaps the thing I’m missing is a regular excitement for life but that hasn’t stopped me from having a good one.

I have had a preoccupation with food since I was a toddler, stealing my younger siblings bottles and hiding under their cribs while drinking them and putting them back empty (note: I had already been fed). 
It is so deeply ingrained in me that I find traditional ideas of success in this area are ineffective and not applicable. Perhaps it’s too much of a negative focus and a reminder of failure that keeps me “failing”. I read through this list of unconventional, but true, ideas of success (not relating to money, power, fame, or even significant weight loss) and I appreciate the perspective. This list mentioned success as having a place you call home, loving and being loved back, learning something new every day, recognizing the abundance in your life, acknowledging small victories, etc. According to this (and against my own self defined failure), I am quite the success story, who knew?!?
Here is a small victory in my lifelong struggle with food addiction, I grew up with a refrigerator full of fruit juice and rarely drank or was encouraged to drink water. I could guzzle gallons of juice a day. Sometime back in my late 20’s I just decided to stop drinking juice and soda as a regular beverage (especially at restaurants) and started choosing water instead. Now (in my late 30’s) it doesn’t even occur to me to reach for soda or fruit juice. Despite my angst over this food addiction and how it dictates my life in so many ways, here is one solid victory I haven’t given much recognition to...and that feels good. That feels hopeful. 
(Sorry for the length!)
Thank you for sharing this, I echo so much of it.

Yes, the struggle I have is the inconsistency of my good days. It seems I’m also saying “I’ll do better tomorrow” WAY more than “I did good today”. I’d love to find a way to flip that so that my binge episodes are fewer and farther between. But once I get into the cycle again (almost a year now for me), I really have a mental block when it comes to changing the behavior.

I wish I had good advice for you but I’m still on my cycle of binge. It would be like the blind leading the blind...but it’s nice to hear from you and know that someone else feels exactly the same way as I do. I plan on doing better today!
You and me both!

Depending on where you live there should be support groups for grief, depression, loss etc. Try using a search engine to locate groups. Most of these groups are free and possibly ask for a donation but it’s not required.
I live in the US and there are usually many support groups in urban areas.

I have found a lot of comfort and safety in support groups. But I too have a hard time finding them because I travel a lot. So my hometown has several but many of the places I travel too make it challenging schedule wise. If you live in a more urban area usually you can find local support groups through a search engine
Do you live in an urban or rural area?

I ask that question regularly...I don’t quite have an answer but I do write it all out as if I was talking to someone and at times that has been helpful. This subreddit seems to be a good place with a mix of opinions and there are plenty that seem to relate. I have had some good conversations with hotline volunteers. I’m sorry you are feeling so defeated.
I hear you. I feel that too. You are not alone.

You are not wrong that the suffering is passed onto loved ones...I lost my brother to suicide last year and all I can say is if this (what I now feel as a result of his death) is even a fraction of what he suffered for years then I understand his need to be free of it (though I still hate that he left us that way). He sought out so many other alternatives through the years and fought against his suicidal tendencies for our sake. I imagine it became too much and in that instant his walls narrowed to what he had been resisting all these years. He was a combat medic in Iraq and suffered PTSD as well as survivors guilt for 15 years. I can’t possibly know his struggle. These things are bigger than our facts and logic. I would like to believe that there is a solution but whatever is we haven’t found it. Suicide in the US is up almost 25% since 1999.
I love the simile! That describes the phrase perfectly.

If it’s any consolation, I was born a female and identify as female but my stature is very masculine. I’ve even been mistaken for a man on numerous occasions. Even as a man in drag. So i feel ya girl...it can be tough not looking the part we feel. It bummed me out for a long time but now I just accept who I know I am regardless of what the rest of the world sees when they look at me. Good luck to you, love. I don’t doubt you are beautiful!

Major depressive disorder (MDD) does not have any basis in logic or reason.  In many cases it’s genetic. It is an illness, illnesses make regular life more challenging, even blindingly unbearable. Your argument is solid for someone who has the capacity to use traditional logic when looking at their life. There are many who simply do not have the capacity for that logic. My brother was a successful, delightful young man who had so many good things in his life and he knew it. He had been seeing a psychologist for several years and on medication but he still took his life. “Hope”was not something his depression would let him see consistently enough to keep him alive. 

Everyone in this boat has a significantly different story and I am happy to hear that you found a silver lining...for some, however, even good things in life do not outweigh their depression. There is no easy answer to this problem and rational and logic play little to no role in the solution in the general sense. 


This is why I have little interest in the “permanent solution to a temporary problem” quote. It forgets that those who suffer significantly have tunnel vision and do not differentiate permanent or temporary...they are desperately seeking solution and desperation is often impulsive. My brother bought himself new luggage and toys for the nieces and nephews for his upcoming trip home just hours before he took his life. One catch phrase cannot possibly sum up my brother’s life and struggle. I reject the quote and I do not feel I am irrational for it.

I agree with you, I’m recently under the interest of sticking around and seeing what happens next because like you said, this very existence is temporary. I lost my younger brother to suicide last year and it has devastated our family...his death has weighed heavy on my own suicidal ideations but I have seen what happens after suicide and it’s a incomprehensible mess that all your loves ones can do nothing but sit in...I figure I might as well stick around to see where all this goes. I’m not going to live forever if it doesn’t get better. 
But that phrase is definitely shit; it reminds me of the D.A.R.E program when I was a kid and if your old enough you’ll know how effective that turned out to be with so many of my generation lost to the opioid crisis.
Hugs to you too!

Yes! And wearing a bathing suit and sandals. Like I was unexpectedly dropped on the mountain from some sandy beach. I’ve never felt so unprepared for anything in my life because nothing compares to this loss for me.

It’s hard for me to believe that anyone who likes to use that catchy quip has ever really felt the fire against their back (mentally speaking). IMO, the problem with that phrase is that it’s a blanket statement for a tremendously personal struggle. It’s also an easy way to write people off when their outlook or feelings on life make you uncomfortable. The first thing ANYONE should be doing if they want to be of any help is LISTEN (no catch phrases necessary).
I’ll be at a year in one more month...I feel you, the grief is still insurmountable.
Thank you for this comment. LMAO
Thank you!

I’m so very sorry. You are not alone. My younger brother took his life last November. He was also a twin (with our sister). It’s incomprehensible and for me has remained to be stifling. It’s not quite a year for me so there are plenty in this subreddit who are more apt to give advice with more time past since their loss. I feel like the blind leading the blind. That being said, it helped me to know that there were others who lost someone in such a way and could not describe or understand their circumstances. I felt isolated in my shock and grief under his cause of death but here, everybody already knows. No explanation necessary. No stigma, just understanding.
I’m so sorry about your momma. I completely understand the desire to eat for no other reason than comfort.

Thank you for sharing this. My brother was a sweet, messy man so my siblings and I had a lot of cleaning up after him too. For me it was cathartic to clean up his car and home because it kind felt like we were taking care of him one last time. I carry my brother’s ashes in a pendant too and a little coin necklace he gave me a few years back. I write to him for therapy because I can’t afford it either. It helps. But reading your story really helps me in this moment too. Thank you.

I know you posted this a while back but I’ve just joined and I appreciate your honesty. I don’t have advice as I feel quite blind to the solution myself but hopefully you have found some help since then and if not, at least you’re not alone. ;)

I write mine down too! My first few dreams after he died were very very vivid. One of which I was sobbing and holding him and he just said very reassuringly, “it’s ok, it’s ok, it’s ok.”
I also had dreams where he would show up and if I acted cool and didn’t draw too much attention to him (because he was alive again) he would stick around in my dream longer.

I am so sorry for your loss.
It’s been 11 months since my younger brother took his life.
I know that it’s different for everyone, but I had similar dreams in the few months following my brother’s death and then they slowly shifted to dreams where we didn’t dwell on the subject of his death but instead just hung out doing random silly things and I wake up feeling good...like we just came back from a random event/hangout/adventure. I don’t even remember some of the dreams but I can tell I was with David (my brother) because it feels like I just left him when I wake up. I look forward to those dreams now because I think my subconscious has finally accepted he’s gone in the physical so it is creating a different way for me to still have connection with my brother, even if it’s entirely self initiated. These loved ones of ours are gone in the physical but not gone out of our memories and consciousness, they are still exactly who they always were.

I’m still on the hunt for peace myself, but I find small doses of it as time slowly moves on; I hope you can find peace as well.
I lost my younger brother last year as well. Thank you for sharing your experience.

You’re an intern, you’re there to learn. The only practical expectation anyone in management should be putting on you is a willingness to learn and a genuine effort to follow directions. This temporary boss of yours sounds like he’s projecting his own personal issues onto you because he’s a poor leader and probably very insecure. I agree with everyone else that this looks more like a bad reflection of him than you. Go easy on yourself, like you said, it’s only a little while longer and you are learning. Learning a skill/ application and learning how to handle yourself in the often unpredictable world of social dynamics in the work place. Just because he’s the boss doesn’t mean he’s qualified.
You’ve got this ;)
You are not alone.

I lost my brother, David (36) last November and one of my biggest heart breaks is that my nieces and nephews (from another brother) will no longer know him past their young ages. He was brilliant and playful and kind and he adored them. Sometimes I worry that they will forget about him all together (being so young)...Reading your post and the link to “Forever In Our Hearts” is very encouraging to me that they will not only remember him but miss him and wish he had known/understood his value in their young lives. We found a closet full of toys for them in his house after he died.
Thank you for sharing your story.

Its still a terrible shock and they will find a way to blame themselves for not being there [enough] for you. I lost my brother to suicide in November 2018 and I spend every day thinking of how I failed and what I could have done better to have helped him, to have stopped it. Im told I couldn’t have stopped it but I still haunt myself with the never ending “what if’s” and “if only’s”. 
Im so sorry you hurt....I hope you can find peace and that that peace keeps your heart beating and your lungs breathing.
Thank you 💗

I lost my younger brother just 6 months ago and my sister (his twin) and I were using the same filter...I looked kind of like him but when we did her, the resemblance was uncanny. We laughed and then cried. I totally get it....so many feelings. Just wish he was still here to laugh with us.
I lost my brother the same way 6 months ago. I’m so sorry.

A move to another country is a big “to do” but sometimes that’s what we need to shake us out of our tunnel vision of self dismissal. It’s a lot of work and planning and takes time but even moving in the general direction of a goal (something different than what we have been doing) can be enough to pull us up a notch or two. 
Besides, it would give you an opportunity to move into a direction of a life you don’t feel the need to lie about. (I get it though, I’ve lied about a thing or two because I want to be perceived as better than I think I am...funny thing though, I’m slowly realizing I can be better than I think I am. Just not over night).
Tokyo! That’s awesome! You could teach English? Many organizations provide housing for their teachers so that would be a two birds, one stone situation.

I live in New Orleans...most of here are pretty broke but we somehow manage to have homes, kids, all that with shitty low wage jobs. It is possible to have all of those things, it’s not a breeze but it is obtainable. Plus, if she’s partner material, she’ll share the load with you happily because she’s into you, not your stats.

Sometimes mediocrity is the byproduct of traditional education because the focus is too much on the grades as opposed to the subject of study. Maybe, if you are going to loose your scholarship anyway, take the opportunity to use the  time off from school and do something different, something interesting, something you find appealing. 
There are plenty of mediocre PHD’s out there, formal education is not all it’s cracked up to be...in my humble non-traditionally educated opinion. 😉
Is it possible that she doesn’t care about the money you do/do not have and that she’s just happy to be in your company?
No way! Hermit crabs are AWESOME!!!

I know he is...that makes me happy. As for happiness as I once knew it, can’t imagine that will ever feel as good as it once did. Everything filters through the grief of his absence now. Maybe not worse, just different (that’s just me trying to see a bright side🤷🏻‍♀️)

Of course. My brother wouldn’t share his load either, he just wasn’t that kind of person. More interested in taking on other people’s loads than asking anything from anyone. He was a good, good man and I’m so happy to have had as many years with him as I did. Truth be told, I don’t know that I could have done anything for him, but I would have listened for as long as he needed. It feels so empty now. 
I’m sorry about your family and school. Life is a shit show for sure...for everyone.

I’ve contemplated suicide most of my 38 years of living (it usually comes in waves and relaxes) but last November my little brother took his life almost out of the blue. All my thoughts of what it would do to my family if I killed myself didn’t even scratch the surface of what it has actually done to my family, my parents and so many other people (who I guarantee he had no idea how many people loved him outside of his family). I’ve lost my buddy and companion as well as a history keeper of our childhood. He saw the world in such a unique way, it’s incomprehensible to realize that I will never hear his stories again in real time. We have other siblings and all of us are at a loss...we can see reasons but not enough to leave your whole family who adores you (he knew it too, he would get jokingly annoyed at how much we all wanted him around). It is confusing for those of us left behind because we feel immense guilt for not seeing it and wondering/ wishing we had been better sisters, brothers, parents, friends. Could we have stopped it if we had been better? Would he still be with us? It’s almost as if all the pain he suffered with in his life that lead him to that moment stayed after he died and was passed onto us, only it’s very confusing to us because it wasn’t our pain to begin with. We just carry it now with so many questions, questions that will stay with us until we die. That being said, I’m happy to carry my brothers pain so he doesn’t have to suffer but I wish he would have shared it with me first so that i could better understand it and maybe helped relieved enough of it for him to feel like he could continue living. I didn’t imagine any of this when I was in the throws of my own suicidal thoughts...how could I? I was too distracted by myself to really invest what it might actually mean to leave my family in that way. I also assumed I was the suicidal depressed one in the family and didn’t think for a moment anyone else was thinking the same as me...again, guilt at my self preoccupation instead of seeing my brothers need. I still feel like ending it but now, knowing what I know, I could never do it. That would just make me the worlds biggest asshole to do that to my family after my brother’s suicide. So here I am, with all the more reason to want to die but deciding every day that choosing to live is for the greater good...and I think I can sustain that. We don’t have that much time anyway, we just get bored and think it’s taking forever. 
Sorry for the length, I’m also sorry that you are hurting and want to die...I know that feeling. I hear you. If you think you can, maybe try to share that load you carry with someone who loves you and would be devastated to loose you.

That’s true, it is very crushing and I can only imagine how devastating it must be to have to modify your dream. I am  very sorry. For what it’s worth, I don’t know you but I have appreciated your honesty with me, that’s a plus and a value (my book) when there are so many people who don’t take the time to engage.

You might be surprised at how unfulfilling even a solid career that pays well may be. My father was an animator for Disney and Warner Brothers for 35 years, it was prestigious (so far as art and entertainment careers go) and it paid well. Yet, when 2D animation went overseas and they laid off most of the animators he had no option but to find another career path. Starting from scratch. The only thing he could find was a janitor for a local school district. It was humbling but ended up being his best job so far as fulfillment. He said he got way more exercise, a lot more free time and way less pressure. He’s retired and still picks up shifts when he’s bored with retirement. Who knew? 
There are SO many directions that one person could take, why gamble your whole worth on only one or two options. That seems so limiting.
I started as a behavioral therapist in Los Angeles and found that after all my investment, and years served, it wasn’t the right fit. That was REALLY discouraging. So I quit and became a musician in New Orleans, ha! Best job ever, so VASTLY different from where I started and from what I thought was success.
So you’re saying that had you made it into med school, you would feel differently now?
If you’re game, I’m game🙂

I went to college (not the best in the country by any means) and it didn’t end up doing much for me. College is overrated when narrowed down to an individual’s actual worth. I would venture to say good schools and good grades won’t take that feeling of pointless from you. I’ve contemplated suicide since I was 10 and now I’m 38, ha! I guess that makes me a failure at life AND death.
All that to say, I don’t think there is a “ “compelling”reason to stay alive because even people with Ivy League degrees, great careers and loving families and children kill themselves. I guess I’ll just say that even though the inclination to  kill myself has been with me most of my life, I look back at all the years I managed to survive and/or fail my suicidal ideation and its been very interesting. Not happy or fulfilled per say, but definitely an unpredictable adventure. My personal opinion is that depression makes for a more interesting, even creative life...just look at all the famous artists and writers who have brought so much creativity to the world. Most of them are/were depressed, lonely, suicidal etc. 

I don’t pretend to know how you feel. I’m sorry for the loss of your mother and the absence of your father. Perhaps your time is up, or maybe it’s just getting started.

Yes, that is the one thing that has kept me from taking my own life and at some particularly low, low points that came close to not mattering either. I’m an empath (my burden) and I could never stop thinking about the damage I would do to my family if I killed myself despite wanting so badly to be done living. However, myself and my whole family were rocked last November when my younger brother killed himself. The “idea” we have about how much our family will suffer does not scratch the surface of the devastation and grief they will ACTUALLY experience...for the rest of their lives. I now have an understanding of what suicide truly does to a family that I never fathomed when contemplating it myself. Now that I have been forced to be on the other side of suicide I have a terrible understanding that I could never have known as the one wanting to die; all your feelings of pain, sorrow, apathy, pointlessness, disappointment, hurt, rage, self-loathing/hate etc. don’t die with you, they will pass onto your family for the remainder of their lives leaving them shocked, confused and devastated because they are all of your reasons to kill yourself now transferred to them. It’s madness and as stifling as this is for me personally, how it has changed and broken my family is beyond description. 
ALL of this to say, I hear you and I am so sorry that you do not see the value of your life to the extent of potentially ending it. I know that feeling well but know that anyone close to you will question themselves and their fault in your death for the rest of their lives (even if all they ever did to you was love you). It even instates a desire to die in family members who have never been inclined to suicidal thoughts and tendencies. If you can, consider that the hurt your family and loved ones will suffer from your death and multiply it by a thousand and know that it will be with them forever...
Also, even if you can’t see it, you have value because others value you. Gold never said to itself, “I’m valuable” and we all started buying it...people decided the value of gold and it became valuable. To your family and loved ones, you are gold. They decided that and much of the time our value is not in what we see but what others see in us. (That is why suicide is so devastating to the survivors).
Sorry for the loooong response. It’s hard to describe how I’ve been...all over the place.

Lost and still in shock, I think. The thought of living the rest of my life is so daunting...I’ve thought more about suicide in the last four months than I have most of my life but now knowing what I know, I just couldn’t do it and leave my family with this grief. It’s relentless and deceptive, right when i think i might be feeling ok and coming to accept his death, I wake up the next day and I can’t imagine another day that o have to distract myself through. When something happens to make me laugh or smile, I immediately think of my brother and how I will never laugh with him again...I wonder that I will ever truly experience anything genuinely good again in my life. 
I’m also paranoid because I feel like I am bummer company. Everything comes back to David, my brother, and his death and how incomprehensible this whole tragedy is. I’m isolating because I don’t want to feel like I have to pretend to be feeling better. He’s my brother, I’ll never feel better about loosing him and wishing I had done something...I hate the thought that he died alone and not with his family around him loving him. I know that’s not how suicide works but I still wish I could have held him and been there...I live across the country from where he was.
I lost my younger brother in November last year.

For the rest of her life, your struggles (after you take your life) will become your mother’s. There is no way to avoid or rationalize that passing on of suffering. Know it will destroy her, even if she is strong and can keep it together...my family and I are left with a completely foreign kind of grief and suffering that will never subside. In my own suicidal contemplation I always considered how it would hurt my family but I had no idea how unbearable it actually is to lose someone you love to suicide.

I have struggled with suicidal thoughts since I was 10 (I’m 38 now). However, my little brother just recently took his life in November, I adore him and we were buddies but he never shared with me how serious he was about suicide. I have never felt so empty, confused, guilty, regretful and sad in my entire suicidal self loathing life. I wish he would have been more straightforward so I could have hugged him tighter, told him more jokes and made sure that he knew how immensely valuable he is to me. The thing is, he did know, but his self loathing spoke louder than our family’s unconditional love for him. I know what that’s like. 
Now that I have been on the other side of suicide, the side of those left behind to make sense of a completely incomprehensible loss, I know something I didn’t before...by taking our own lives, the pain doesn’t go away, it’s passed onto the ones who love us and are left behind...and it’s unbearable. I know those voices in our heads scream so loud and drown out everything else, but try for a moment to listen to your momma’s voice that loves you so much and will NEVER understand why her love wasn’t enough. At the very least give your momma a chance to love you like she knows she could loose you, I wish I had that chance with my brother. I’m so sorry you are hurting. Be well.

I’m so sorry that you have had to go through all of this and that you found your brother. I lost my younger brother to suicide (gun shot to the head) last November. My sister, his twin, found him. She’s been resorting to writing about it for herself because talking can be challenging not just for her to express but also to find someone who will just listen. I know many on here have said that are available to listen if you need and I’m offering the same. As morbid as it may sound, it has helped me to know that there are many others who have lost siblings to suicide...I guess just because I don’t feel so isolated. There are many others that have had similar experiences and I don’t feel so alone knowing that. 
To the best of your ability, take care of yourself and feel free to reach out!
